title: Wolcott Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Wolcott wells have a 235-foot median depth, with fractured mountain bedrock affecting yield, construction and cost.
h1: Wolcott, Colorado Well Depth, Yield and Cost Guide
intro_html:
Wolcott sits in mountain terrain where most permitted wells draw from unnamed fractured-bedrock aquifers. Records within 5 miles show a median well depth of 235 feet, a median reported yield of 15.0 gallons per minute, and a wide range of drilling results. The records include 557 permitted wells, but only 252 are recorded as constructed, so the dataset is useful for local patterns rather than a guarantee for a particular lot.

For a purchase or new build, look beyond the nearest well. Check neighboring permits, construction reports, static water levels, access for a rig, septic layout and the legal status of the intended household use.

sections.heading: Wolcott’s well depths reflect fractured mountain ground
sections.html:
Wolcott wells vary considerably. The median reported depth is 235 feet, while the middle half runs from 86 to 382 feet. That spread matters when requesting a drilling bid: a contractor may need to price a substantially deeper hole than the median if the local fracture system does not produce water early.

The depth mix gives more context. 26% of reported wells are under 100 feet, 35% fall from 100 to 300 feet, and 31% are from 300 to 600 feet. The 90th percentile is 580 feet, and the deepest record is 3,800 feet. Those extremes are not a prediction for your lot, but they show why a fixed shallow-well assumption is risky in Wolcott.

sections.heading: What Wolcott wells produce for a home
sections.html:
Reported yield is stronger than the depth variation might suggest. The median is 15.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half between 10.0 and 15.0 gallons per minute. In the records, 56% of wells report more than 15 gallons per minute, while 37% fall between 5 and 15 gallons per minute.

Low-producing wells are present but not dominant: 6% report from 1 to 5 gallons per minute, and 1% report less than 1 gallon per minute. Yield is not the same as storage or water quality. A buyer should ask for the well construction report, pump test information and any required storage or treatment design. A household-use exempt well is generally limited to 35 gallons per minute under Colorado rules.

sections.heading: Static water levels and the local water picture
sections.html:
Only 22 wells in the records report a static water level, so the water-level sample is limited. Among those reports, the median depth to water is 225 feet, with the middle half from 80 to 275 feet. That range affects pump setting, electrical requirements and the cost of lifting water to the house.

The permit history does not by itself show a reliable long-term water-table decline. It shows permits issued across several decades, but the available static-level records are too few to treat the series as a trend for all of Wolcott. Ask for a recent measurement from the subject well and nearby wells. In fractured granite or gneiss, nearby properties can encounter different fractures and different water levels even across a short distance.

sections.heading: Who has drilled around Wolcott, and when
sections.html:
Wolcott’s permit history is concentrated in the 1990s, when 209 permits were issued. The record also includes 5 from the 1960s, 23 from the 1970s, 54 from the 1980s, 108 from the 2000s, 41 from the 2010s and 22 from the 2020s. The newest permit year is 2025.

The most frequent driller in the records is Golden Eagle Drilling Corporation (Shelton, Joe Wayne), associated with 192 wells. Shelton Drilling Corporation (Shelton, Wayne) appears on 38, and Steve Shelton Drilling, Inc. (Shelton, Steve) on 31. This is useful history, not an endorsement. Confirm current licensing, insurance, availability and the scope of any proposal.

sections.heading: A Wolcott well budget starts with the rock
sections.html:
The local cost model assumes fractured mountain bedrock, including granite and gneiss. The typical drilling rate is $65 to $100 per foot. At the 235-foot median depth, the drilled hole works out to about $15,300 to $23,500.

A finished system costs more than the hole. Including the pump, tank, trenching and electrical, the modeled total at the median depth is about $21,300 to $35,500. Treat that as planning guidance, not a fixed quote. Depth, casing, grout, access, drilling conditions, water testing, storage and site distance can change the final price. Ask exactly what the bid includes and what happens if the driller has to continue past the planned depth or abandons a dry hole.

sections.heading: Risks to investigate before building or buying
sections.html:
Environmental due diligence deserves attention around Wolcott. Within about 10 miles of the area, the mapped records include 16 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 16 historic mine features and 7 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. These mapped sites do not prove contamination at a specific well. They do justify a site-specific water test and a review of land and groundwater history.

Also check for low yield, a dry hole, poor casing or grout, and a pump that cannot handle the static water level. Septic setbacks, reserve areas, driveway access and building placement must work together before drilling. In an over-appropriated basin, an augmentation plan may be needed for some uses. Confirm the DWR permit’s allowed use rather than assuming a domestic permit supports every planned use.

sections.heading: A practical lot checklist for Wolcott
sections.html:
Before closing, pull the nearby DWR permits and separate constructed wells from applications or incomplete records. Compare depths, reported yields, static levels, aquifer descriptions and use types near the parcel. The local records are mostly tied to unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifers, with 520 wells in that category, plus 16 Morrison wells and 11 Mancos wells. There are 0% Denver Basin aquifer wells in this dataset.

For a new build, have a driller review rig access and likely casing depth, then have a septic designer confirm the available area before finalizing the house site. For an existing home, inspect the pump, pressure tank, electrical system and treatment equipment, and obtain a current laboratory water test. Edwards, Eagle, Avon, Fulford, McCoy and Gypsum provide useful comparison areas when reviewing nearby permit history, but the subject parcel still needs its own evaluation.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Wolcott, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported well depth within 5 miles of Wolcott is 235 feet. The middle half runs from 86 to 382 feet, 90% are at or below 580 feet, and the deepest record is 3,800 feet. The range reflects fractured mountain bedrock, so nearby wells do not guarantee the same depth on a new lot.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Wolcott?
faq.a: The local model uses $65 to $100 per foot for fractured mountain bedrock. At the 235-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at $15,300 to $23,500. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching and electrical is modeled at $21,300 to $35,500. Access, casing, grout and extra depth can change the quote.

faq.q: How much water do Wolcott wells produce?
faq.a: The median reported yield is 15.0 gallons per minute, and the middle half is 10.0 to 15.0 gallons per minute. Records show 56% producing more than 15 gallons per minute. Lower yields still occur: 6% report 1 to 5 gallons per minute and 1% report less than 1 gallon per minute.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Wolcott?
faq.a: Safety cannot be determined from a permit record alone. Within about 10 miles, mapped records include 16 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 16 historic mine features and 7 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Those sites do not prove a problem at your well, but a laboratory test and review of the property history are appropriate before drinking the water.

faq.q: Are Wolcott wells running out of water?
faq.a: The available records do not establish a reliable area-wide water-table decline. Only 22 wells report static water levels; their median depth to water is 225 feet, with a middle half from 80 to 275 feet. Because fractured-bedrock conditions vary, request a current static-level measurement, well history and pump information for the specific property.
